12:22 SGTInvesting
China's economic slowdown is deepening:

China's retail sales rose just +0.4% YoY in October, the 3rd-lowest reading since December 2022, and well below the expected +0.8% growth.

This marks a sharp deceleration from a +1.1% YoY increase in September.

Retail sales are now on pace to end the year with their weakest growth since 2020.

Meanwhile, industrial production grew +4.8% YoY last month, down from +5.5% in September, and the slowest expansion in 3 months.

Furthermore, fixed-asset investment fell -8.1% YoY in the first 10 months of 2026, its biggest decline since the 2020 pandemic.

In October alone, investment dropped -16.9% YoY, the largest decline on record outside the pandemic.

China's domestic demand continues to deteriorate.

@ · 20 Nov 2026, 23:51 SGT
$NBIS has been getting absolutely crushed lately. But before you panic and sell, understand who is actually running this company.

His name is Arkady Volozh.

In 1989, before the Soviet Union collapsed, Volozh was already developing search technology. In 1997, a year before Google was founded, he co-founded Yandex.

Over the next 25 years, he transformed Yandex into a technology empire worth tens of billions of dollars. He built one of the few search engines in the world capable of beating Google in its home market.

Yandex expanded into cloud computing, AI, autonomous vehicles, e-commerce, and ride-hailing. In 2011, Volozh took the company public on Nasdaq.

Then everything changed in 2022. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Volozh was sanctioned by the EU and stepped down from Yandex.

In 2024, Yandex sold its Russian businesses for approximately $5.4 billion. The international businesses remained with the Dutch parent company, which became Nebius Group.

At around 60 years old, when most executives would consider retirement, Volozh decided to build another technology giant.

This time, his focus was AI infrastructure.

Since then, Nebius has secured multibillion-dollar agreements with Microsoft and Meta, attracted investment from NVIDIA, and positioned itself as a major player in the AI infrastructure industry.

Think about that. He built a company capable of challenging Google, lost control of its Russian operations to geopolitics, and started building another multibillion-dollar technology business.

The stock can drop 10%, 20%, or 40%. That doesn’t erase decades of execution.

I’m not bullish on $NBIS because I expect the stock to go up tomorrow.

I’m bullish because I believe Arkady Volozh is building his second technology empire.

And I believe the market is underestimating what he can accomplish.

Inflation in Japan is accelerating:

Japan's CPI inflation excluding fresh food jumped +2.1% YoY in September, its highest YoY increase since December 2025.

Since May, Japan's CPI inflation has risen +0.6 percentage points.

Furthermore, CPI excluding fresh food and energy surged +2.4% YoY, its largest YoY increase since January.

Overall CPI inflation rose +2.1% YoY last month, its highest reading since November 2025.

This comes as the Iran War continues to fuel inflationary pressures in Japan, which relies heavily on imported food and energy.

Meanwhile, Japan's major food and beverage companies planned price increases for 3,153 items in October, the 2nd consecutive monthly reading above 3,000 for the first time since July 2023.

Inflationary pressures in Japan are broadening again.

The US economy is gaining momentum.

BREAKING: This past week's -10.4% drop in the Nasdaq 100 was one of the rarest weekly declines in 40 years.

Of the last 2,133 trading weeks, just 11 saw declines of this magnitude or worse.

That's 0.52% of all weeks, a 3.27 standard deviation move based on the historical mean and volatility.

Of course, market returns exhibit "fat tails," meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution would predict.

However, even accounting for the fact that extreme market moves are more common than traditional statistical models suggest, this was a historically rare selloff.

Volatility returns when markets least expect it.

One of the best investing tips I've received is to treat your stock portfolio like an actual business.
Investors should micromanage their positions the same way Jensen micromanaged his subordinates.

Applying to current market conditions, I see absolutely no issues with realising profits/losses in ultra low conviction positions rather than praying to see the H1 highs again.

How do you know which ones these are? Clue - you open your portfolio and think "Why on Earth did I buy this stock, and why the hell do I still own it?"

IMO this type of reflection should be done weekly...but we're here now after a major correction and it's never too late to get started.

Having this type of active reflection each week will fundamentally transform your investing habits.

*Appreciate there's also a "fun" element to all this too, so ask yourself: Am I holding too many 'fun' positions and not enough 'sleep easy' positions?

Investor positioning in copper is cratering:

Speculative investors sold -$1.3 billion in Comex copper futures in the week ending November 10th, marking the 7th consecutive weekly sale.

This group includes hedge funds, commodity trading advisers (CTAs), and other institutional investors.

Since September 22nd, they have sold a cumulative -$10.8 billion.

This brings long speculative investor positioning down to ~$5.2 billion, its lowest since October 2025.

Meanwhile, copper futures fell -5.3% on Wednesday, marking their largest daily decline since July 2026.

Copper prices are now down -18.2% from their September peak, to $5.67 per pound, their lowest level since April.

The copper market is seeing a massive shift in sentiment.

The semiconductor trade is still popular among fund managers:

39% of global fund managers said "long global semiconductors" was the most crowded trade, according to a BofA survey of 169 fund managers overseeing $461 billion in assets conducted between November 6th and November 12th.

This marks the 6th consecutive month that semiconductors have held the top spot.

However, this figure is down from the 82% peak recorded in July this year.

Meanwhile, “Short China Stocks” ranked 2nd for the first time, with 14% of respondents identifying it as the most crowded trade.

By comparison, "Long Magnificent 7" and "Short Treasuries" were considered the most crowded trades just by 12% and 10% of fund managers, respectively.

Investor appetite for semiconductor stocks remains strong.

Gold is caught up in the liquidity crunch.

1. VIX above 35: buy aggressively
- High-beta tech, growth, small caps
- Every single time the VIX spiked above 35 since 2018 was a generational buying opportunity. COVID bottom. Oct 2022 bottom. Tariff crash. If you bought when everyone else was panicking, you made a fortune.

2. VIX 25 to 35: start scaling in
- Quality tech, financials, industrials, cyclicals
- This is where smart money starts building positions. Not all at once. Gradually. The fear is real but the opportunity is bigger.

3. VIX 15 to 25: hold
- Balanced: tech + defensives, dividend growers
- This is normal. Stay positioned. Don't chase, don't panic. Let your winners run.

4. VIX below 15: reduce exposure
- Rotate to: utilities, healthcare, staples, bonds
- This is when everyone is comfortable. Nobody is hedging. Nobody is worried. That's exactly when you should be.
- Every major crash in market history was preceded by the VIX sitting below 15 for weeks.

For anyone who’s been keeping up with the streams, you know I put a collar on my Nvidia position on Monday before earnings.

This was around $155.

I sold the $165 calls for this week and used that premium to buy the $150 puts. The premium covered 77.5% of the cost and I ended up paying a $0.90 debit for the hedge.

I have just exercised those puts and sold my Nvidia position at $150.

I started buying this name during DeepSeek and ended up getting to an average of $120. Ever since the Jensen news came out, I have felt incredibly uneasy about the position, especially going into earnings given the name couldn’t break out with Jensen on the call so I had no reason to believe it could break out without him.

The risks are simply too high with Nvidia even though the valuation obviously is cheap beyond imagination, assuming the earnings growth continues to be true. The credit backstops, China issues, Jensen not being there…these things could work out but the risk to them at this moment obviously is much higher than normal. The investigation itself is an annoying overhang on the stock regardless of their growth.

I’ve bagheld various names down and stuck with the story, many times with Nvidia in early 2025, but I was not willing to baghold this name because of Jensen’s affairs. I think the majority of retail are in this name between $120-$140 and now basically have to make a decision if they think things will change or if this company continues forward without Jensen.

Nvidia can obviously bounce from here, but it’s less about the price action up. It was cheap at $180 and cheap at $150. I wouldn’t care about buying this back at a higher price than I sold, but there would need to be a reason. Just not interested in this until Jensen comes back, if he does.

03:47 SGTInvesting
What's rather unique about the market correction over the last 45 days is that the market is no longer waiting on President Trump to intervene.

In every major market downturn since January 2025, President Trump has had the ability to intervene and mark a bottom. And, that's almost always what happened.

This includes the trade war, Iran War, Greenland situation, US-China tensions, interest rates, Venezuela, and more.

In our X Article earlier today, we named this financial backstop the "Trump Put."

Minutes ago, President Trump held a press conference and mentioned Iran, Nvidia, China, and Ukraine, but never markets.

With the shift in political power in the US, the era of the "Trump Put" appears to be nearing its end.

The erosion of this backstop for financial markets partially explains why selling pressure has been so strong this week.

This will be a major adjustment for investors.

I covered this earlier in Jan regarding PCB bottlenecks with photonics + $AMZN Kuiper / $SPCX starlink supply chains.

But as an update, it like other industries outside of AI are really starting to feel the pain now too.

Global Electronics Association: "Is issuing this Industry Alert on escalating shortages across the printed circuit board (PCB) supply chain.

Companies in automotive, industrial, medical, defense, and telecommunications report longer lead times and difficulty securing supply as AI absorbs scarce capacity, effectively putting production at risk"

The association meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. The association urged buyers to plan ahead for supply constraints and manufacturers.

Hyperscalers like $AMZN already planned ahead of time taking stakes in Gold Circuit Electronics (2368) for supply procurement...

But can't say the same about other industries procurement (medical industry is probably not used to competing with hyperscalers over the same supply lol).

The resulting shortages of critical materials, including CCLs and fibreglass cloth, are squeezing supplies for consumer electronics.

TLDR: same bottleneck, same timeline for 2028. It's just interesting to see association warnings about it impacting medical to defense industries.

So there's incremental information that it's become an industry wide allocation issue.

I also think it's helpful to see escalating shortages + broadening... so it might show the selloff is starting to look very disconnected with fundamental demand.

"that the ROI for companies to buy their own GPU environments and run their own models is starting to come to the forefront"

Shared some of my overall thoughts on Semi’s few weeks ago
Venu @Venu_7_ · 13 Oct 2026, 11:57 SGT
Sharing some of my thoughts on the recent weakness across AI and semiconductor names.

One thing I've always believed is that technicals often tell us about strength or weakness before the fundamentals and headlines catch up.

Looking at the broader semiconductor and memory theme, the recent price action is becoming concerning. I was expecting memory & semi stocks to build the right side of their bases, but looking back, the weakness we saw around June-July may have been an early warning sign.

We had a decent bounce over the last three months, but instead of building stronger bases, several names are now testing or losing their 50-day and 100-day moving averages.

On top of that, $NVDA is showing signs of a failed breakout, while $TSM, $SMTC, $NBIS and $LITE have also seen failed breakout attempts. Meanwhile, $AVGO has slipped below its 200-day SMA.

When stocks spend months consolidating, you want to see accumulation, higher lows, improving relative strength, and eventually a breakout. Instead, we're seeing failed breakout attempts, lower highs, and key moving averages being tested across multiple leaders in SemiConductor sector mainly.

One or two stocks showing weakness is normal, but when several leaders within the same theme start showing similar technical deterioration, that's something worth paying attention to.

A LOT of poor price action across semiconductor and AI names lately.

Does this mean the AI infrastructure cycle is over? Not at all! I still believe AI infrastructure has significant long-term growth potential.

But there's a difference between being bullish on a theme over the next 3-5 years and ignoring deteriorating price action in the short term.

As much as I'm bull at heart, you can't ignore what the market is telling you. Sometimes being patient and selective is just as important as being aggressive when the opportunities are there.

That being said, software, healthcare, crypto, and several other themes are holding up relatively well. Even some international markets, like Brazil, are showing encouraging signs of strength.

Just because one theme is correcting doesn't mean the entire market is falling apart. Capital can rotate from one area to another, and new market leaders can emerge while previous leaders consolidate.

The opportunities haven't disappeared. They're just not necessarily in the same places they were a few months ago!

Markets appear to be wrongly interpreting Chinese eSSD cuts as deteriorating demand and NAND oversupply.

Phison CEO commentary today + more context behind $SNDK / Kioxia selloff regarding Trendforce revisions:

- "Pua attributed China's recent enterprise SSD demand slowdown to GPU shortages since November 2026"

- "Without GPUs, additional purchases offer little value, prompting some companies to sell server components on the spot market to recover cash"

(for context enterprise SSDs are growth driver for NAND)

- "Chinese cloud giants nevertheless plan substantial GPU prepayments, temporarily tying up capital and delaying procurement of other components."

- "the principal challenge in 2027 would be insufficient supply rather than weakening demand, with persistent AI shortages potentially prompting further procurement and inventory accumulation."

Markets seemed to have wrongly interpreted this as demand destruction + pricing collapse.

When Phison CEO attributed it to
-> GPU shortages
-> causing procurement timing mismatch
-> Chinese CSPs needed capital for GPU prepayments, so liquidation in inventory (causing spot price volatility)
-> timeline shift in order procurement

TLDR: delayed procurement from GPU shortages. there were actual order cuts, but this is deferred procurement not structural demand weakening.

Chinese CSPs needed capital for GPU prepayments so they liquidated other inventories in the meantime.

Phison says its inventories are insufficient for anticipated 2027 demand and it's sees this as an opportunity for NAND accumulation.

It's interesting the bottleneck in China migrated back to GPUs though.

Gold $GLD is a perfect reminder that even the strongest market leaders eventually break down. And what happened to gold could offer an important lesson for semiconductor stocks.

When gold experienced that massive deleveraging candle on January 30, 2026, it was the first major warning sign. Once that kind of leverage gets flushed out, rebuilding momentum isn't easy.

And when one of the world's most important commodities loses its 200-day SMA after a historic multiyear rally, that's a serious warning that the previous uptrend coming to an end.

Let me explain why.

Once an asset enters a Stage 4 downtrend, nobody knows where the bottom will be. That's exactly why many of us, including myself, suggest avoiding falling knives during Stage 4.

Instead of trying to predict the bottom, I prefer waiting for the price to stop declining and begin moving sideways, which is how a Stage 1 base starts developing.

Since my earlier post in June, gold has experienced further selling pressure and down 15% from June. I think we could eventually find support near the 200-week SMA and potentially spend years building a new Stage 1 base.

Look at what happened between 2011 and 2016. Gold experienced a roughly 45% drawdown and took years to establish a meaningful base.

I'm not suggesting we'll see the exact same timeline, but I wouldn't be surprised if gold goes through a similar process of consolidation before its next major uptrend.

And for the record, I'm still a long-term gold bull!

Now, here's why I'm bringing up gold in the first place.

I'm seeing some similarities in the semiconductor ETF $SMH.

$SMH has already declined roughly 33% from its record closing high and experienced significant selling pressure.

When a major index or ETF experiences an extraordinary run over three to four years, it's not unusual for that advance to be followed by a significant drawdown and a prolonged period of consolidation.

Sometimes these corrections last months. Sometimes they take years. That's one of the reasons I place so much importance on the 200-day moving average. It helps me identify whether the longer-term trend is still intact.

Now, before someone says gold and semiconductors are completely different assets, I agree!

Semiconductor companies generate earnings, have different fundamentals, and operate in a completely different industry.

But that's not the comparison I'm making.

I'm comparing how human emotions, institutional positioning, and market cycles show up in price charts.
Technical analysis is essentially the study of market participants' behavior through price and volume. Fear, greed, leverage, accumulation, distribution, and expectations all influence price action.

And those patterns can appear across different asset classes.

Another interesting observation is the 200-week SMA.

I was charting $NVDA and $GOOGL today, looking at how they behaved during previous major market corrections.

Consider some of the historical periods:
- 2018 market correction
- 2020 COVID crash
- 2022 tech bear market
- April 2025 tariff-related selloff

The 200-week SMA has acted as an important long-term support reference during several major drawdowns.

That doesn't mean every stock will reach it, or that it will always hold.

I'm certainly not predicting that $SMH, $NVDA, or $GOOGL must decline to their 200-week moving averages.

I'm simply highlighting an important historical reference that investors should keep in mind when evaluating potential downside risk.

And here's the bigger lesson.

Right now, everyone seems to be waiting for an oversold bounce, a V-shaped recovery, or the exact market bottom.

But markets don't recover just because we want them to. A new uptrend begins when selling pressure eases, buyers regain control, and price action starts confirming improving conditions.

Until then, patience, discipline, and following your own investment & Trading framework matter far more than predicting the next move.

You don't need to catch the exact bottom to make money in the markets.

And you certainly don't need to call a bottom every single day just so you can eventually claim you were right.

You don't need to catch the bottom to build wealth. You need the discipline to survive the downtrend and the patience to participate in the next uptrend.
Venu @Venu_7_ · 10 Jun 2026, 22:34 SGT
Want to study how major leaders top out?

Study the $GLD chart.

• After forming a massive 12-year cup & handle, Gold broke out in January 2024 and rallied nearly +170%. This is exactly why I pay close attention to big, multi-year bases.

• I call this framework "4 Bases & 4 Runs." After breaking out of multi-year or multi-decade bases, many leaders tend to advance in a series of bases followed by powerful runs. I've seen similar behavior in names like $GLD, $SLV, and even $MSTR in 2024.

• During these uptrends, leaders often consolidate and backtest key moving averages like the 21-day EMA and 50-day SMA before beginning their next leg higher.

• The real lesson comes at the end. On the fourth run, notice the climactic volume spike - the highest since the initial breakout. The very next day, price gaps down sharply. That's often a sign that liquidity is drying up and the move is becoming exhausted.

It doesn't mean the asset crashes immediately. Dip buyers can still show up. But more often than not, the easy money phase is over, and the stock or commodity enters a much longer period of consolidation before its next major cycle begins.

Study how leaders begin. Study how they end.

The exits are often hidden in plain sight.

If you found this helpful, feel free to share.

True, I've looked at biotech, physical AI, cybersecurity, space, and others... But I still have conviction that optics is the most compelling opportunity.

If you look at Elon Musk $SPCX (Mesh acquisition), $MRVL (Lumentum acqusition), Samsung Electronics photonics foundry push...

SK Hynix CPO push + PIC IP acqusitions... it's endless.

Private VCs are still heavily pouring funds into upcoming optical companies.

Supply procurement is accelerating... from $SOI selling $1.2B in agreements, in a single quarter (from $25M revenue/quarter). To $COHR signing $20B in LTAs, to $LITE selling out of 2029 capacity.

Actions about where the industry is heading is the biggest signal over valuations crashing.

Even if you stress test aggregate capex slowdown or accelerator flood vs. grid constraint/permitting downside:

- There's an economic incentive to improve GPU efficiency and power utilization. (eg. Lambda's CPO data suggests enough power savings to support ~4.5% more GPUs)... for power constrained DCs.

- There's an economic incentive to reduce expensive HBM4 requirements in certain cases (eg. $MRVL estimating up to 30% savings through optical memory pooling)... for memory constrained inference.

While for economic upside in these companies:

-> Optical networking, and their upstream materials like substrates and lasers represent a relatively small fraction of total AI cluster BOM.

-> At the same time, optical content goes up...while selling prices of that content rise nonlinearly as well (lasers 10x+ selling price from pluggable to CPO.)

In terms of the future winners:

- Many low end players eg. 400G/800G, module assemblers etc. don't capture the same scale in economics from the NPO/CPO transitions... compared to laser suppliers, fiber array suppliers, modulator suppliers, or companies in the ELS/optical engine stacks.

- Tracking capacity expansion is also important... but US/China supply chain birufration will improve scarcity economics of Western players (eg. China optical transceiver bans past 3.2T)

But even if aggregate AI capex slows, there's a strong economic incentive to accelerate optical deployments and to make every iota of compute more economically valuable.

Visibility keeps increasing, demand keeps increasing, strategic value keeps increasing, while valuations crashed. NFA, but I'd personally, argue this is an opportunity.

Extremely bullish on industry transition to light.

I'm hearing multiple things from industry executives:

1. Potential $NVDA employee exodus if Jensen doesn't come back soon.

Many senior management and engineers can easily retire after Nvidia stock appreciation over the years.

They don't need to continue working sitting on millions in equity. But they continued to work because Jensen was a visionary leader.

Under new interim CFO (former CFO), it gives an excuse for that lot of people to finally quit soon. A pay bump or hiring $ARM CEO isn't going to change that.

So you have generational talent leaving.

2. Loss of confidence in $NVDA future growth (Jensen was the moat).

What I'm hearing is that Jensen understands heavily top-down architectures, and it's this magical discretionary element that doesn't get covered in media.

When cuda, network, and $NVDA internal teams are arguing, Jensen made the final choices around heavily nuanced discretionary decision about where Nvidia + AI ecosystem ends up going:

Then everyone followed. The supply chain, capital, agreements, and faith.

You also can't suddenly replace the trust that local Taiwanese factories build with Jensen over the years if you bring in external CEOs, or even internal executives.

It was transformational bet after bet after bet after bet that Jensen made until Nvidia became a former $5T+ company.

3. $NVDA is not that technologically far ahead of others. It's not a 5 year lead, but months ahead to a year in different areas.

Jensen was accelerating all of that. Longer Jensen is gone, the longer Nvidia and its competitive ecosystem decays, beyond the current near-term roadmaps.

Nvidia's greatest moat was Jensen Huang making high-stake architectural decisions and accelerating capital, suppliers, + the industry to rally around his vision.

There's a massive loss of confidence in $NVDA with Jensen gone.

From extreme euphoria to extreme fear in just five months. Welcome to the stock market!

June 2026:
- Stocks going to the moon.
- Triple- and even quadruple-digit YTD returns.
- AI stocks looking unstoppable.
- Euphoria & leverage everywhere.

November 2026:
- Hedge funds blowing up.
- AI stocks getting crushed and down 50-70%
- Jensen's departure and $NVDA down 40% from ATH.
- Nasdaq down roughly 15% from its ATH.
- Fear and pessimism everywhere.

Five months. Two completely different market environments.

That's how quickly sentiment can change in the markets.

Markets change, but human psychology never does.

During euphoria, greed makes everyone believe the good times will last forever. During corrections, fear makes everyone believe the pain will never end.

The greatest advantage isn't predicting the next market move. It's controlling your emotions when everyone else is losing control.

How Would William O’Neil Read This Market?

Nasdaq $QQQ is trading below its 200-day SMA, and 16 of the 23 market leaders I'm tracking are also trading below their respective 200-day SMAs.

Here's what stands out:
- 8 distribution days in the past 25 sessions, signaling significant institutional selling pressure.
- Most former leaders have lost their long-term trends.
- A handful of names, including $AMD, $ANET, $MSFT, $AMZN, and , have shown relative strength.

What would O'Neil's playbook suggest?
- Avoid aggressive new buying during corrections.
- You should be raising cash for past few weeks and cut losses before they become significant.
- Build a watchlist of stocks showing relative strength and institutional accumulation.
- Watch for a Follow-Through Day from Day 4 onward, supported by strong price and volume.
- Start with smaller positions and increase exposure only when the market and your positions confirm the uptrend.

One important lesson I've learned:
- Relative strength during a correction is a clue, not a buy signal.
- Some of the strongest names can still fail when the broader market remains weak.

The goal isn't to catch the exact bottom. It's to identify the next group of market leaders when conditions improve.

The biggest winners are often born during market corrections, but that doesn't mean you have to buy them during the correction.

Identify them early. Buy them when the market confirms.
